hook.text: Flip a light switch and billions of electrons start marching instantly.

buildup.text: Electrons carry a tiny negative charge. When they move together, that's current.

discovery.text: Current is measured in amperes — one amp equals a coulomb of charge per second.

twist.text: Each electron moves slowly — only millimeters per second through copper wire.

climax.text: The push travels near light speed, but the electrons themselves crawl.

punchline.text: Current is the crowd moving, not any single runner.

quiz.question: What does one ampere of current represent?
options: One electron passing a point per second
One coulomb of charge passing a point per second
One volt of pressure per ohm of resistance

hook.text: Copper carries current easily. Rubber blocks it completely. Why the difference?

buildup.text: In conductors, outer electrons roam freely between atoms like a shared pool.

discovery.text: Insulators grip their electrons tightly. No free electrons means no current flow.

twist.text: Semiconductors sit in between — they conduct only under certain conditions.

climax.text: Every circuit needs both: conductors to carry current, insulators to contain it.

punchline.text: Loose electrons flow. Tight electrons stay put.

quiz.question: Why do conductors carry current easily?
options: They are always made of metal
Their outer electrons move freely between atoms
They have more protons than insulators

hook.text: Engineers draw current flowing one way. Electrons actually move the opposite way.

buildup.text: Benjamin Franklin guessed current flows from positive to negative. He was wrong.

discovery.text: Electrons carry negative charge and move from negative to positive terminal.

twist.text: By the time we knew, all equations were built on Franklin's convention.

climax.text: So engineers kept conventional flow. The math works either way.

punchline.text: The arrows point the wrong way — and nobody cares.

quiz.question: Why do circuit diagrams use conventional current flow?
options: Electrons actually do flow from positive to negative
All equations were built on that convention before the truth was known
Conventional flow is more accurate for AC circuits

hook.text: Rub a balloon on your hair and it sticks to the wall. That's static charge.

buildup.text: Friction transfers electrons from one surface to another. One gains, one loses.

discovery.text: The imbalance creates a voltage difference. Opposite charges attract.

twist.text: Lightning is static discharge on a massive scale — billions of volts.

climax.text: Static can destroy microchips. Factories ground workers to prevent damage.

punchline.text: Charge at rest is harmless — until it jumps.

quiz.question: What causes static electricity?
options: Magnetic fields pull electrons from atoms
Friction transfers electrons between surfaces, creating charge imbalance
Heat causes electrons to vibrate and escape their atoms

hook.text: One coulomb of charge is 6.24 quintillion electrons. A staggering number.

buildup.text: Charles-Augustin de Coulomb studied the force between charges in the 1780s.

discovery.text: Double the charge, quadruple the force. Double the distance, quarter the force.

twist.text: This inverse-square law mirrors gravity. Charge and mass follow the same math.

climax.text: Coulomb's law is the foundation of all electrostatics calculations.

punchline.text: Charge obeys the same rules as gravity — just far stronger.

quiz.question: What happens to the force when you double the distance between charges?
options: It doubles
It drops to one-quarter
It stays the same

hook.text: Touch a faulty appliance and current can flow through your body. Grounding stops that.

buildup.text: A ground wire connects metal cases to the earth via a buried rod or pipe.

discovery.text: If a wire touches the case, current takes the easy ground path — not through you.

twist.text: The earth is a huge conductor. It absorbs stray current without voltage rise.

climax.text: A breaker trips when ground current spikes, cutting power in milliseconds.

punchline.text: The ground wire is the escape route current takes instead of you.

quiz.question: What does a ground wire do in a faulty appliance?
options: It increases the voltage to blow the fuse faster
It gives stray current an easy path to earth instead of through a person
It stores excess charge in the metal casing

hook.text: One equation rules all simple circuits: V equals I times R.

buildup.text: Voltage is the push, current is the flow, resistance is the opposition.

discovery.text: Double the voltage and current doubles — if resistance stays the same.

twist.text: Georg Ohm published this in 1827 and was ridiculed. Colleagues rejected it.

climax.text: Today every electrical engineer uses Ohm's law daily. It never fails in linear circuits.

punchline.text: V = IR. Three letters, infinite circuits.

quiz.question: According to Ohm's law, what happens if you double the voltage?
options: Current halves
Current doubles, if resistance stays the same
Resistance doubles automatically

hook.text: Voltage is like water pressure in a pipe — it pushes current through a wire.

buildup.text: A battery creates a voltage difference between its terminals using chemistry.

discovery.text: One volt means one joule of energy moves one coulomb of charge.

twist.text: A Van de Graaff generator reaches millions of volts but delivers tiny current.

climax.text: High voltage isn't deadly on its own — it's voltage times current that kills.

punchline.text: Voltage is the push. Without it, nothing flows.

quiz.question: What does one volt represent?
options: One electron moving through one meter of wire
One joule of energy per coulomb of charge
One ampere flowing through one ohm

hook.text: Every material fights current flow. That fight is called resistance.

buildup.text: Thin wires have more resistance than thick ones. Longer wires resist more too.

discovery.text: Resistors are components designed to add precise amounts of resistance on purpose.

twist.text: Color bands on a resistor encode its value — each stripe is a digit.

climax.text: Without resistors, current would surge unchecked and fry every component.

punchline.text: Resistance isn't the enemy — it's the traffic cop.

quiz.question: Why are resistors used in circuits?
options: To generate voltage from nothing
To add precise resistance and control current flow
To store energy for later use

hook.text: A 100-watt bulb and a 10-watt LED both light a room. One eats ten times more power.

buildup.text: Electrical power equals voltage times current: P = V × I.

discovery.text: One watt means one joule of energy used per second. Watts measure consumption rate.

twist.text: Double the current through a resistor and power quadruples — P = I²R.

climax.text: That's why thin extension cords overheat. High current in small wire wastes power as heat.

punchline.text: Power is how fast energy flows — not how much exists.

quiz.question: Why does doubling the current quadruple the power in a resistor?
options: Because P = V × I and voltage also doubles
Because power depends on current squared: P = I²R
Because resistance automatically doubles with current

hook.text: Walk around any closed loop in a circuit. The voltage rises and drops always sum to zero.

buildup.text: A battery lifts voltage up. Resistors drop it back down. Every volt is accounted for.

discovery.text: This is energy conservation — what goes in must come out around the loop.

twist.text: Complex circuits have many loops. KVL applies to every single one simultaneously.

climax.text: Engineers use KVL to solve circuits with dozens of components and branches.

punchline.text: Around any loop, voltage gained equals voltage lost.

quiz.question: What does Kirchhoff's Voltage Law state?
options: Current entering a junction equals current leaving it
The sum of all voltage rises and drops around a closed loop equals zero
Resistance increases proportionally with voltage

hook.text: At any junction in a circuit, current in equals current out. None is lost.

buildup.text: If 5 amps flow into a node and 3 amps leave one branch, 2 amps leave the other.

discovery.text: This is charge conservation — electrons don't pile up or vanish at a junction.

twist.text: KCL works even in circuits with thousands of nodes. Every node must balance.

climax.text: Together, KVL and KCL let you solve any linear circuit completely.

punchline.text: What flows in must flow out. Charge has nowhere to hide.

quiz.question: What does Kirchhoff's Current Law require at a junction?
options: Voltage must be the same on all branches
Total current entering must equal total current leaving
Each branch must carry equal current

hook.text: Old Christmas lights had one fatal flaw — one bulb dies, they all go dark.

buildup.text: In a series circuit, components line up end to end. Current has only one path.

discovery.text: The same current flows through every component. Resistances add up directly.

twist.text: Voltage splits across each resistor — more resistance gets more voltage.

climax.text: Break any link and the entire circuit stops. That's the weakness of series.

punchline.text: One path, one current — and one point of failure.

quiz.question: What happens to total resistance in a series circuit?
options: It equals the smallest resistor value
Individual resistances add up to give the total
It equals the average of all resistors

hook.text: Modern Christmas lights stay on when one bulb burns out. Parallel wiring does that.

buildup.text: In parallel, components connect across the same two nodes. Each gets full voltage.

discovery.text: Current splits among branches. More branches means more total current drawn.

twist.text: Total resistance drops below the smallest individual resistor. More paths, less opposition.

climax.text: Your home wiring is parallel — each outlet gets full voltage independently.

punchline.text: Many paths mean no single point of failure.

quiz.question: What happens to total resistance in a parallel circuit?
options: It equals the sum of all resistors
It drops below the smallest individual resistor
It equals the largest resistor

hook.text: A camera flash takes seconds to charge but releases all its energy in a burst.

buildup.text: A capacitor stores charge on two metal plates separated by an insulator.

discovery.text: Capacitance is measured in farads. Most real caps are micro or picofarads.

twist.text: Capacitors block DC but pass AC — they charge up and stop, then reverse.

climax.text: They smooth power supplies, filter noise, and set timing in oscillators.

punchline.text: A capacitor is a tiny rechargeable bucket for electrons.

quiz.question: Why do capacitors block DC current?
options: DC has too much voltage for the plates to handle
They charge up fully and stop current once the plates reach supply voltage
The insulator between plates only conducts AC

hook.text: An inductor resists sudden changes in current. It's electrical inertia.

buildup.text: A coil of wire builds a magnetic field when current flows through it.

discovery.text: Energy is stored in the magnetic field, not in charge like a capacitor.

twist.text: Cut the current suddenly and the field collapses, producing a voltage spike.

climax.text: Inductors pass DC freely but choke high-frequency AC. The opposite of capacitors.

punchline.text: Inductors hate change — they fight any shift in current.

quiz.question: How does an inductor store energy?
options: In an electric field between its plates
In a magnetic field created by current flowing through its coil
In chemical bonds within its core material

hook.text: A diode lets current flow one direction and blocks it the other way.

buildup.text: It's a semiconductor junction — P-type meets N-type silicon.

discovery.text: Forward-biased, current flows freely. Reverse-biased, almost nothing passes.

twist.text: LEDs are diodes that emit light. The color depends on the semiconductor material.

climax.text: Rectifiers use diodes to convert AC to DC — inside every phone charger.

punchline.text: A diode is a one-way street for electrons.

quiz.question: What is the primary function of a diode?
options: To amplify weak signals into strong ones
To allow current in one direction and block it in the other
To store energy in a magnetic field

hook.text: A switch is the simplest circuit component — open means off, closed means on.

buildup.text: Mechanical switches use metal contacts that physically touch or separate.

discovery.text: A relay is a switch controlled by another circuit — a small signal controls big power.

twist.text: Early computers used thousands of relays. Each click was a logic operation.

climax.text: Transistors replaced relays — smaller, faster, no moving parts to wear out.

punchline.text: On or off — every digital device starts with a switch.

quiz.question: What does a relay allow in a circuit?
options: It converts AC to DC power
A small signal controls a switch that handles much larger power
It stores energy in a magnetic field for later use

hook.text: Batteries produce DC — current flows in one direction, always steady.

buildup.text: DC voltage holds constant over time. Plot it and you get a flat line.

discovery.text: Electronics love DC. Chips, LEDs, and sensors all need clean, steady voltage.

twist.text: DC is hard to transmit far. Voltage drops quickly over long wires.

climax.text: Edison championed DC power. He lost the war of currents — but DC rules electronics.

punchline.text: DC is simple, steady, and perfect for everything small.

quiz.question: Why is DC hard to transmit over long distances?
options: It can only travel through copper wire
Voltage drops quickly in long wires due to resistance losses
DC current reverses direction after a few kilometers

hook.text: Your wall outlet delivers current that reverses direction 50 or 60 times per second.

buildup.text: AC voltage rises, peaks, falls to zero, goes negative, then repeats.

discovery.text: Transformers only work with AC. They step voltage up or down effortlessly.

twist.text: High voltage AC travels hundreds of miles with minimal loss. DC couldn't do that in 1890.

climax.text: Tesla and Westinghouse won the current war. AC powers the world's grid.

punchline.text: AC won because transformers make long-distance power cheap.

quiz.question: Why did AC win the 'war of currents' for power grids?
options: AC is safer than DC at all voltages
Transformers can easily change AC voltage for efficient long-distance transmission
AC uses less copper wire than DC

hook.text: North America runs on 60 Hz. Europe uses 50 Hz. Both work fine.

buildup.text: Frequency is how many complete cycles AC completes each second, measured in hertz.

discovery.text: Higher frequency means faster reversals. Radio waves oscillate millions of times per second.

twist.text: Mismatched frequency causes clocks to run fast or slow. Your microwave depends on it.

climax.text: Grid operators keep frequency rock-steady — a fraction of a hertz off triggers alarms.

punchline.text: Frequency is the heartbeat of every AC system.

quiz.question: What does 60 Hz mean for an AC power system?
options: The voltage is 60 volts
The current completes 60 full cycles every second
Power travels at 60 meters per second

hook.text: A 120V outlet actually peaks at 170V. The 120V number is the RMS value.

buildup.text: AC swings from peak positive to peak negative. Its average is zero — useless.

discovery.text: RMS means root mean square — it equals the DC voltage that delivers the same power.

twist.text: RMS is always about 70.7% of the peak value for a sine wave.

climax.text: Every voltage rating on an appliance is RMS. It's the number that matters for power.

punchline.text: RMS tells you what AC actually delivers — not what it promises.

quiz.question: Why is RMS used instead of peak voltage?
options: Peak voltage is impossible to measure accurately
RMS equals the DC voltage that delivers the same heating power
RMS is always exactly half the peak value

hook.text: Factories don't use single-phase power. They need three-phase for heavy loads.

buildup.text: Three AC waves, each 120 degrees apart, share the same wires.

discovery.text: The three waves always sum to a constant — power delivery is perfectly smooth.

twist.text: Three-phase delivers 73% more power than single-phase with the same copper.

climax.text: Every industrial motor, data center, and power line uses three-phase today.

punchline.text: Three waves beat one — smoother, cheaper, and more powerful.

quiz.question: Why does three-phase power deliver smoother energy?
options: The voltage is three times higher than single-phase
Three waves offset by 120 degrees always sum to a constant
Three-phase uses thicker wires that reduce resistance

hook.text: Your phone charger takes AC from the wall and outputs DC. Rectifiers do the conversion.

buildup.text: A half-wave rectifier uses one diode to block the negative half of each AC cycle.

discovery.text: A full bridge uses four diodes to flip the negative half positive. Smoother output.

twist.text: Even after rectification, the output is bumpy. A capacitor smooths the ripples.

climax.text: Every laptop, phone, and LED light has a rectifier and filter inside its power supply.

punchline.text: Four diodes and a capacitor turn AC into DC — everywhere.

quiz.question: What does a full-bridge rectifier do?
options: Converts DC to AC for power transmission
Uses four diodes to flip both halves of AC into positive DC
Doubles the voltage of an AC signal

hook.text: Need 3.3V from a 5V supply? Two resistors can split the voltage for you.

buildup.text: Two resistors in series share the supply voltage based on their ratio.

discovery.text: Output voltage equals supply times R2 divided by R1 plus R2. Simple ratio math.

twist.text: Connect a load and the divider's output voltage drops — it's not a power supply.

climax.text: Voltage dividers set bias points for transistors and read sensor values everywhere.

punchline.text: Two resistors, one ratio — voltage on demand.

quiz.question: What is a limitation of a voltage divider?
options: It can only divide by exactly half
Output voltage drops when a load draws current from it
It only works with AC voltage sources

hook.text: How do you measure a tiny change in resistance? Balance a bridge and watch it tip.

buildup.text: Four resistors form a diamond. A meter reads the voltage across the middle.

discovery.text: When balanced, the meter reads zero. Any imbalance reveals the unknown resistance.

twist.text: Strain gauges use Wheatstone bridges — tiny deformation changes resistance detectably.

climax.text: Every digital scale and load cell uses this 1843 invention daily.

punchline.text: Balance the bridge and the invisible becomes measurable.

quiz.question: How does a Wheatstone bridge measure resistance?
options: It measures the current through a single resistor
It detects voltage imbalance in a four-resistor diamond circuit
It compares resistance to a fixed voltage standard

hook.text: A circuit with 20 resistors and 5 sources can be reduced to one voltage and one resistor.

buildup.text: Thévenin says any linear network can be replaced by a single source and series resistor.

discovery.text: Find the open-circuit voltage and the equivalent resistance seen from two terminals.

twist.text: Norton's theorem does the same with a current source and parallel resistor instead.

climax.text: Engineers use Thévenin to analyze complex circuits one section at a time.

punchline.text: Any circuit, two terminals, one equivalent — that's Thévenin.

quiz.question: What does Thévenin's theorem produce?
options: A set of differential equations for the circuit
An equivalent circuit with one voltage source and one series resistor
A frequency response plot for the circuit

topics.title: Superposition: One Source at a Time

hook.text: A circuit has three voltage sources. Solving them all at once is a headache.

buildup.text: Superposition says: turn off all sources but one and solve. Repeat for each source.

discovery.text: Add the individual answers together. The sum is the total response.

twist.text: Turning off a voltage source means replacing it with a wire. A current source becomes open.

climax.text: Superposition only works in linear circuits — no diodes or transistors allowed.

punchline.text: Solve one source at a time and add the results. Done.

quiz.question: What does 'turning off' a voltage source mean in superposition?
options: Setting it to its maximum value
Replacing it with a short circuit (wire)
Removing it and leaving the circuit open

hook.text: A capacitor doesn't charge instantly. It fills up along a smooth exponential curve.

buildup.text: The time constant τ equals R times C. It sets how fast the cap charges or discharges.

discovery.text: After one τ, the capacitor reaches 63% of full charge. After five τ, it's 99% full.

twist.text: This same curve describes camera flash timing, touch screen response, and audio filters.

climax.text: RC circuits are everywhere — from debouncing buttons to shaping radio signals.

punchline.text: R times C tells you how fast a circuit responds.

quiz.question: What percentage of full charge does a capacitor reach after one time constant?

hook.text: Play music through a speaker and you hear bass and treble. Circuits can separate them.

buildup.text: A low-pass filter blocks high frequencies. A high-pass filter blocks low ones.

discovery.text: The cutoff frequency is where the output drops to 70.7% — the half-power point.

twist.text: Band-pass filters combine both — only a chosen slice of frequencies gets through.

climax.text: Equalizers, radio tuners, and noise cancelers all rely on frequency filtering.

punchline.text: Every circuit has a frequency it loves and ones it ignores.

quiz.question: What happens at a filter's cutoff frequency?
options: The output drops to zero
The output drops to 70.7% of the input — the half-power point
The filter switches from low-pass to high-pass mode
